title: Glass of Water and Card
description: Because of surface tension and air pressure, when a card is placed on a glass of water and the system inverted, the card will stay attached to the cup. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the equipment on the lab table. Pour water into the cup.  (It does not have to be full.)  Place the card on top of the cup making sure that the cup does not hang off the edge of the card.  Holding the card to the cup, flip the system over.  Carefully remove your hand from the card.  The card should remain attached to the cup.
notes: This demonstration may require some practice ahead of time.
equipment: Cup, Index Card, Beaker of Water

title: Magdeburg Hemispheres
description: This demonstration shows the effects of atmospheric pressure.  Initially, the plates pull apart easily.  When the air is pumped out from between them, the two plates are difficult to pull apart because of the atomospheric pressure. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Connect the plates to the vacuum cart with the valve open.  The plates will pull apart easily. Put the plates together and turn on the vacuum pump.  Be careful of the alignment so that you get a good seal. Once the air is pumped out, close the valve and turn off the pump.  The plates will be very difficult to pull apart. Open the valve and the plates will fall apart.
notes: None
equipment: Magdeburg Plates, Vacuum Cart

title: Pop Can Collapse
description: The demonstration dramatically shows a difference in pressure outside and inside an aluminum can.  When the can is inverted and dunked in the water, the steam inside the can quickly cools.  This rapid drop in temperature causes a drop in pressure.  Since the opening of the can is underwater,  there is no way for outside air to enter the can.  It cannot support the pressure, so the walls collapse. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Fill the large bowl with water.  Put a small amount of water in the aluminum can.  (Just enough to cover the bottom.) Place the can on the hotplate and heat it until steam builds up in the can.  Using the tongs quickly flip the can over and into the bowl of water.  The can will be crushed.
notes: This demonstration may require a little practice to master.
equipment: Hotplate, Water, Empty Aluminum Can, Large Bowl or Beaker, Tongs

title: Disk Rolls Up a Ramp
description: This disk has a mass hidden inside of it. When started in the correct position on a ramp, the disk appears to move up the ramp as this hidden mass moves downward.
setup: Set the ramp on the lab table with the disk next to it. Place the wooden disk at the bottom of the ramp with the screw for the hidden mass inside at the 1:30 position (if there was a clock on the face of the disk; see the first photo).  Release the disk and it will roll up the ramp.
notes: This demo may require a little practice.
discussion_questions: Will increasing the mass of the disk cause the demo to fail or work better? What about the hidden mass? | How would a steeper hill change the results? Will it fail to roll uphill (assuming static friction remains)?
equipment: Weighted Wooden Disk, Short Ramp

title: Friction and Normal Forces
description: This demonstration shows how normal force affects friction.  As mass is removed from the top of the block reducing the normal force, static friction is overcome and the block begins to slide.
setup: Set up the equipment as shown in the image above. Remove masses stacked on the block until the system slides.  The forces can then be discussed.
notes: None
discussion_questions: Does adding or removing mass before the block slides change the friction force on the block? How about the friction coefficient(s)? | What would cause the coefficients of friction to change?
equipment: Klinger Magnetic Mechanics Kit, String

title: Walking the Spool
description: A spool with a string attached can be moved in different ways depending on how the force is applied.  If the string is pulled horizontally, the spool with roll toward you.  If the string is pulled vertically, the spool will move away.  There is also an angle that when pulled at, the spool will spin in place. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place spool on lab table.  Make sure it won't roll off. If the string is pulled horizontally, the spool will roll toward you.  If the string is pulled more vertically, the spool will move away.
notes: This demo may require a little practice.
discussion_questions: What does the free-body diagram of the system look like? | Does the mass of the spool matter? The coefficient of friction?
equipment: Spool with String Attached

title: Gravity Well
description: This demonstration is used to visually display the orbital motion of a planet around a star in its gravitational field. A ball orbits in the well, picking up speed as it gets closer to the center.  This helps students visualize Kepler's Second Law. * Equipment seen in the leftmost video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup. New Set-up available upon request (below), but need at least three days for set-up and organization
setup: Connect the PVC pipes together into an octagon. Place sheet across pipes and use clamps to hold it in place. Hang hangers and masses from paperclips attached to center of well.Place the ball in the well, give it an initial tangential velocity and release to see orbits.  The ball will orbit and eventually speed up and fall into the center of the well.
notes: This demonstration may require a little practice to get the desired orbits.
discussion_questions: If we replaced a large ball with a small one with the same mass, would the orbits change? (Relate to replacing the sun with a solar-mass black hole) | How would the orbit change if you had two equal masses instead of a big and small mass?
equipment: PVC pipes with connectors, Sheet, Clamps to hold sheet, paper clips, hangers with masses, Assorted Balls

title: Air Pucks
description: This equipment can be used to show Newton's Laws, momentum, and collisions.  The pucks glide with minimal friction so they can be used to demonstrate many different phenomenon.  The pucks have bumpers so they can be used to show elastic and inelastic collisions. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the pucks on the demo table. Turn the pucks on using the switch on the bottom. The pucks can be pushed toward each other or one set still and the other pushed towards it to show collisions.
notes: To show Newton's First law, place the puck on the table and give it a push to show it will continue unless acted upon by another force.
discussion_questions: In a head-on collision, why will one puck never go away at an angle? Why must both go off at an angle in order for us to get 2D motion? | When they are of equal mass, a head on collision with a stationary puck stops the first puck. Would increasing the speed change this?
equipment: Two Air Pucks, Webcam (optional)

title: Basketball, Tennis Ball Drop
description: A tennis ball is placed on top of a basketball then dropped from some height.  Because of the transfer of momentum, the tennis ball rebounds very high into the air while the basketball does not. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place Balls on the lab table so they will not roll off. Balance the tennis ball on top of the basketball in the center.  Release the balls and watch them bounce.  The tennis ball will go very high while the basketball does not.
notes: Be sure to perform in a high ceiling area or outside. If the tennis ball is not centered it will fly off to the side. Some practice ahead of time helps with this demo.
discussion_questions: Is the force on the tennis ball higher than the force on the basketball? | Does the ground move in response to the basketball hitting it? Does the Earth?
equipment: Basketball, Tennis Ball

title: Glider Collisions
description: This demonstration shows elastic and inelastic collisions using gliders on an air track.  Some gliders have Velcro on the end so they will stick together after a collision.  Others have bumpers on the end, so they will bounce off each other.  Using these different types of carts and carts of different size, several different collisions can be modeled. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Roll the air track into the lecture hall and plug it in.  Place several gliders on the cart (some with Velcro, some with bumpers and of different sizes). Turn on the air track and place two gliders on it.  Push the gliders toward each other or one glider towards a stationary glider to investigate different types of collisions. Remove the gliders and then turn off the air track when finished.
notes: The mass of the gliders can be recorded as well to add to the discussion.
discussion_questions: If two equal mass objects moved towards each other at the same speed and had an elastic collision, would they stop moving or bounce off of each other? What about an inelastic collision? | We see that if an object hits a stationary object of equal mass, it stops and the other moves at the original speed of the first. What happens if they stick together? | Why do lighter objects tend to bounce while heavier objects tend to keep going? | Are the forces equal between the objects in collisions? Then why do lighter objects get affected more?
equipment: Air Track, Velcro Gliders of Different Sizes, Bumper Gliders of Different Sizes, Scale (optional)

title: Newton's Cradle
description: Several balls are suspended from a frame so that they hang touching.  The balls can be pulled away from the system and released to show different collisions and the transfer and conservation of momentum in each case. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.
setup: Place the apparatus on the lab table.  If using a webcam, connect it to the computer and set it up to view the demonstration. Pull one or multiple balls away from the system, then release them to see how the system reacts.
discussion_questions: Will it ever occur that a different number of balls moves away from one side than hits the other? What would you need to change in order for that to occur?
equipment: Newton's Cradle Apparatus (large, small, or both), Webcam (optional)

title: Water Rocket
description: This demonstration shows conservation of momentum.  A small plastic rocket is partially filled with water then air is pumped into it which compresses the air in the chamber.  When the rocket is fired, the pressure forces the water out at high speed and the rocket flies away. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the toy and water on the lab table. Turn the rocket upside down and pour the water up to the fill line.  Pull back the launcher's slider towards the piston's handle.  Slip the slider onto the rocket (without tipping the rocket over) and make sure it is snug.  Turn the whole assembly upright.  Pump about 15 strokes of air into the piston.  Point the rocket across the room (away from people and objects), and pull back the slider.  The rocket will fly across the room.
notes: Do not point the rocket at anyone or anything! Do not use more than 19 strokes of air. After launch, a little water will spill out onto the carpet.
discussion_questions: Will providing more fuel give the rocket more power? What if we added more air? What if we added more water?
equipment: Water Rocket Toy, Water

title: Equal Mass but Unequal Density
description: Objects of the same mass but different density are set out for viewing and discussion.  The objects all have a mass of 1 kg but have different densities and thus different volumes and shapes.
setup: Place the objects on the instructor's table.
notes: None
discussion_questions: How does this relate to the age-old question: Which is heavier, 1kg of rocks or 1kg of feathers? | In what situations would having a higher density be preferable? | In what situations would having a lower density be preferable?
equipment: 1 kg Brass Cylinder, 1 kg Wooden Block, 1 kg Plastic Puck

title: Unit Vectors
description: These displays can be used to help students visualize the three axes of the Cartesian coordinate system or the right hand rule.
setup: Place the displays on the lab table.
notes: None
discussion_questions: Why is it important to define this convention? Where would trouble occur if we didn't?
equipment: Cartesian Unit Vectors Display, Right Hand Rule Display

title: Away and Back
description: Track the motion of a student using a motion sensor and view graphs of their position and velocity.
setup: Plug the motion sensor into the Pasco interface and connect the interface to the computer.  Open the Pasco data collection software and setup a graph of position vs. time and velocity vs. time.  Place the motion sensor at the edge of the table oriented towards a person.  Press record in the data collection software and have the person walk away from and towards the sensor.  The graphs will populate.  Press stop to end data collection.
notes: Make sure the motion sensor is on the setting for a person walking.  (There is a switch on the unit.) The sensor is not accurate at distances very close to it (< 1m).  For best results use distances of 1 to 8 meters.
discussion_questions: If the student only goes in one direction, can the slope of the position vs. time graph ever change sign? Can the slope of the velocity vs. time graph?How does this change if you were going in both? | How does this change if you were going in both? | How does this change if you were going in both? | What does the slope of each graph represent? | How does average velocity/acceleration appear on a graph? | Can your instantaneous velocity be higher than your average? Can it be lower? | Let's say your average velocity was higher than some speed limit. Could you have been going slower than this limit the whole time?Did anyone ever need to measure velocity directly to know you were speeding? | Did anyone ever need to measure velocity directly to know you were speeding? | Did anyone ever need to measure velocity directly to know you were speeding?
equipment: Demo Computer or Laptop with Pasco Software, Pasco Interface, Motion Sensor

title: Constant Acceleration
description: A glider on an inclined air track is released to show motion at a constant acceleration.  Plots of position, velocity, and acceleration vs. time are displayed to show the relationships between them. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the air track on a lab jack to create an incline.  Connect the motion sensor to the Pasco interface. Connect the interface to the computer. Connect the demo computer to the projector system.  Mount the motion sensor above the air track aligned with the sail on the glider using the ring stand. Open the Pasco data collection software and create graphs of position vs. time, velocity vs. time, and acceleration vs. time. Turn on the air track. Place the glider at the top of the track and hold it in place. Press record on the software and release the glider. The graphs populate. Press stop to end data collection. For a slightly different experiment, start close to the sensor and push the cart up the ramp and let it fall back down.
notes: Level the air track horizontally. Ensure that the motion sensor is in cart mode. (There is a switch on the sensor.) Use a sail on the glider for more accurate data collection.
discussion_questions: Can an object have zero velocity and nonzero acceleration? | Can velocity always be nonzero if you change direction? | What is the difference between acceleration and deceleration? Does it have anything to do with the positive or negative sign of acceleration by itself?
equipment: Air Track Cart, Glider with Sail, Demo Computer or Laptop, Pasco Interface, Motion Sensor, Lab Jack, Ring Stand

title: Constant Velocity
description: A glider is pushed on an air track to show motion at a constant velocity.  A plot of position vs. time and velocity vs. time is displayed. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Connect the motion sensor to the Pasco interface.  Connect the interface to the computer.  Mount the motion sensor above the air track aligned with the sail on the glider using the ring stand.  Open the Pasco data collection software and create graphs of position vs. time and velocity vs. time. Turn on air track.  Place the glider on the track and hold it in place.Press record on the software and give the glider a gentle push.  The graphs populate.  Press stop to end data collection.
notes: Level the air track. Ensure that the motion sensor is in cart mode.  (There is a switch on the sensor.) Use a sail on the glider for more accurate data collection.
discussion_questions: Can a cart be considered going at a constant velocity if it's not moving? | What would an acceleration vs. time graph look like in the case of not moving and in the case of constant velocity? How would they differ? | In a constant velocity situation, how does the instantaneous velocity differ from the average?
equipment: Air Track Cart, One Air track Glider with Sail, Motion Sensor, Pasco Interface, Demo Computer or Laptop, Ring Stand

title: Feather and Coin
description: This demonstration shows howthe presence of airaffects free fall.  If afeather and coin are dropped at the same time, the coin will land first. However, ifthe two are dropped in vacuum, they will land at the same time.
setup: Connect the feather - coin tube to the vacuum pump using the tube. Plug in the vacuum pump to start pumping the tube to vacuum. Seal the tube by turning the knob at the end and disconnect the vacuum pump. Tilt the tube to make the feather and coin fall.
notes: This can be done twice, once before pumping and once after to show the effect of air resistance.
equipment: Feather - Coin tube, Vacuum Pump

title: Picket Fence - Obtaining g
description: A picket fence is dropped through a photogate and a plot of velocity vs. time is displayed.  The bands on the picket fence interrupt the photogate.  Because the picket fence has a known band width, the sensor records the time of the interruption and calculates the velocity.  The slope of this line gives the acceleration which is an experimental determination of g. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Connect the photogate to the Pasco interface. Connect the interface to the computer. Connect the demo computer to the projector system.  Mount the phtotgate to the lab table using the clamps. Open the Pasco data collection software and create a graph of velocity vs. time. Press record on the software and drop the picket fence through the photogate. The graph populates. Press stop to end data collection.  Use the linear fit to see the slope of the line and the calculated value of g.
notes: Be sure the picket fence does not hit the photogate.
discussion_questions: Does this experiment directly measure g? What does it directly measure? | Why do the lines have to be exactly the same?
equipment: Demo Computer or Laptop, Pasco Interface, Photogate, Picket Fence, Clamps

title: Ballistic Cart
description: This demonstration shows that in projectile motion, the horizontal and vertical components are independent. A ball is launched vertically from a cart traveling down a track. The ball flies up into the air and lands back in the cart. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the cart track on the lab table and level it.   Attach the launcher part way down the track. Place the cart on the track with the ball in the cradle and the correct side facing the launcher. Make sure the launcher is aligned with the cart. Push the ball down in the launcher to load the spring. Push the cart down the track. As the cart passes the launcher, it will launch the ball into the air and catch it.
notes: It is recommended to do this demo before either of the other two ballistic cart demos as it provides the basis for the others.
discussion_questions: (before demo) Will the cart catch the projectile? If not, will the projectile fall ahead of or behind the cart? | Why do we intuitively think the ball will fall behind the cart? | We can see what this demo looks like from the outside reference frame. What does this experiment look like to the ball and cart in their reference frame? | How can we relate this to the situation of people inside of a train car? | Let's pretend we were the ones tossing a ball upwards and the cart was the one observing us? How is this situation different from the one we saw in the demo?
equipment: Cart Track, Ballistic Cart with Launcher, Ball

title: Ballistic Cart Acceleration
description: This demonstration shows projectile motion with an accelerating cart. A ball is launched from the cart pulled by a mass hanging over a pulley at the end of the track. The ball travels up in the air but does not land in the cart. * Equipment seen in the picture may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the cart track on the lab table and attach a pulley to the end. Attach the launcher part way down the track. Tie a string to one end of the cart and to a mass hanger with the desired mass. Place the cart on the track with the ball in the cradle and the correct side facing the launcher. Make sure the launcher is aligned with the cart.  Hang the mass over pulley. Push the ball down in the launcher to load the spring. Release the cart down the track. As the cart passes the launcher, it will launch the ball into the air.  Because the cart is accelerating, it will not catch the ball.
notes: It is recommended to do this demo in addition to the original ballistic cart demo as it provides more context.
discussion_questions: (before demo) Will the cart catch the projectile? If not, will the projectile fall ahead of or behind the cart? | Why did this configuration not work when the original ballistic cart did? | What does the motion look like in the cart's reference frame?Bonus: What does the motion look like in the ball's reference frame? | Bonus: What does the motion look like in the ball's reference frame? | Bonus: What does the motion look like in the ball's reference frame?
equipment: Cart Track, Ballistic Cart with Launcher, Ball, Pulley, String, Mass Hanger, Masses

title: Ballistic Cart Incline
description: This demonstration builds upon the idea of projectile motion by adding an incline.  A ball is launched from cart traveling down an incline. The ball still lands in the cart. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the cart track on the lab table and elevate one end using the lab jack. Attach the launcher part way down the track. Place the cart on the track with the ball in the cradle and the correct side facing the launcher. Make sure the launcher is aligned with the cart.Push the ball down in the launcher to load the spring.The cart may be released down the track or pushed up it. As the cart passes the launcher, it will launch the ball into the air and catch it.
notes: It is recommended to do this demo in addition to the original ballistic cart demo as it provides more context.
discussion_questions: (before demo) Will the cart catch the projectile? If not, will the projectile fall ahead of or behind the cart? | How is this situation different from the horizontal ballistic cart? | What does the motion look like in the cart's reference frame? What is the direction of gravity? | Why does this still work even though we're no longer in an inertial reference frame?
equipment: Cart Track, Ballistic Cart with Launcher, Ball, Lab Jack

title: Centripetal Force
description: This demonstration shows centripetal force as a ball is rolled around a circular track.  Once the ball reaches the gap in the track it will fly off in a straight line.
setup: Place the rings and balls on the demo table. Push the ball along the track.  Once it reaches the opening it will fly out in a straight line. This may be done under the document camera or the webcam to aid the students in viewing it.  Graph paper can be placed under the demonstration to help show the straight line movement.
notes: None
discussion_questions: (Before demo) What will the motion look like? | How is this similar to swinging a bucket around on a rope then cutting the rope? | Does the speed of the ball matter? | Does the mass of the ball matter? | How would this change if the track was vertical?In this case, would the speed of the ball matter? The mass? | In this case, would the speed of the ball matter? The mass? | In this case, would the speed of the ball matter? The mass?
equipment: 3/4 Ring, Ball or Marble, Webcam (Optional), Graph Paper (Optional)

title: Dropped Ball vs. Shot Ball
description: A device is used to drop a ball and horizontally shoot a ball at the same time to see which will hit the ground first.  Since both balls have the same vertical acceleration, they can be seen and heard hitting the floor at the same time. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Use the ring stand to set up the ball drop/shot apparatus above the floor. Push the tab back and into the slot to load the spring and prepare the apparatus to shoot the ball.  Put the solid ball in front of the post and the channel ball onto the post behind the spring. Flip the tab up out of the slot to release the spring and launch both balls.
notes: The balls will shoot some distance and roll.  Please be observant of where they go and return them to the lab table.
discussion_questions: (before demo) Which ball will hit the ground first? Why? | (before or after demo) Do the masses of the balls matter?Since air resistance is a thing we have to deal with, what about the two balls does matter? | Since air resistance is a thing we have to deal with, what about the two balls does matter? | Since air resistance is a thing we have to deal with, what about the two balls does matter? | Will the demo change if we shot one ball at an angle upward? What about downward? | Will the demo change if we shot the ball at a faster or slower speed?
equipment: Ball Drop/Shot Apparatus, One Solid Ball, One Ball with a Channel Through It, Ring Stand

title: Galileo's Ramp
description: This demo shows how the distance the cart rolls down the incline increases with even units of time. Chimes are placed at various points along the track.
setup: Place the track between two tables of different height (Or prop one end of the track with something to create an incline) Use ring stands, right angle clamps, and metal rods to position and hang chimes above the track. Set the cart at the higher end of track and let it ride down the track.
notes: Be sure that the cart's wheels spin freely and that they are in the grooves on the track.
equipment: Cart Track, Cart, Chimes, Ring Stand, Right Angle Clamps, Metal rods

title: Roller Coaster Race
description: Two cars race along side by side tracks.  One is on a track with no vertical change.  The other is on a track with hills and a loop.  Both are started at the same time to see which finished first.
setup: Place the roller coaster track on lab table. Place the cars on the track making sure the wheels are aligned in the grooves on the track. Release both cars at the same time to see which finishes first.
notes: Be sure that the cars wheels spin freely and that they are in the grooves on the track.
discussion_questions: Why did the cart going through the longer path finish faster? | What do the position/velocity/acceleration vs. time graphs look like for both carts?
equipment: Pasco Roller Coaster Track (One Straight Track and One Looped Track), Two Pasco Roller Coaster Carts

title: Shoot the Target
description: The system is setup with a projectile launcher aimed at a target some distance away.  When the ball is shot, it travels through a photogate which senses the interruption and releases the target.  As both fall at the same rate the ball travels horizontally and hits the target in the air. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Mount the projectile launcher on the lab table using a clamp.  Mount the photogate across the barrel of the launcher.  Connect the photogate to the control box.  With the control box disarmed, connect the power to it and connect it to the drop box.  Use a ring stand to mount the drop box across the room.  Hang the target from the drop box.  Place a foam block below the target.  Use the laser on the launcher to align the launcher with the target.  (It should be centered on the target as it hangs.)  Place the ball in the launcher and use the rod to push it to the desired range.  Arm the control box.  Pull the string on the launcher to fire the ball and drop the target.  The ball should hit the target in mid air.
notes: Test this demonstration ahead of time to ensure the correct range is chosen. For a more satisfying time of flight of the projectile, a longer cable (20+ ft) will need to be used to attach the control box to the drop box.

If you'd like, go through the other two options first and show that they don't work. Then, you can propose the third option or someone in the class might figure it out by then as well. | To really ask a trick question, don't explicitly mention the third option. If you'd like, go through the other two options first and show that they don't work. Then, you can propose the third option or someone in the class might figure it out by then as well. | To really ask a trick question, don't explicitly mention the third option. If you'd like, go through the other two options first and show that they don't work. Then, you can propose the third option or someone in the class might figure it out by then as well. | Do the masses of the objects matter? | Does the initial velocity of the projectile affect whether or not it will hit?If so, how does it affect it?If not, what does it affect? | If so, how does it affect it?If not, what does it affect? | If so, how does it affect it? | If not, what does it affect? | Where would we need to aim if the falling object starts falling before we launch the projectile? What about after?
equipment: Projectile Launcher with Laser Alignment, Ball, Control Box with Power Adapter, Photogate with Cable, Drop Box with Cable, Target, Foam Block, Ram Rod, Clamps, Ring Stand

title: Breaking Block
description: This dramatic demonstration shows several principles at once.  The massive cinder block is set at rest on a person's chest or stomach.  The much less massive sledgehammer strikes it causing the block to break.  This can be explained in terms of Newton's Laws, Energy, and Pressure. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the cinder block on the persons chest or stomach so that the flat side is facing up. Once the person is ready, count down and swing the sledgehammer to strike the block slightly to the side of the center beam causing it to break.
notes: This demo must be practiced ahead of time for safety reasons. CAUTION: This demonstration is dangerous and is performed at the instructors own risk. This demonstration may also be done by smashing a cinder block on top of a bed of balloons as shown below.
discussion_questions: Why does the person underneath not feel like they were hit by a sledgehammer?Alternatively, why do the balloons not pop? | Alternatively, why do the balloons not pop? | Alternatively, why do the balloons not pop?
equipment: Sledgehammer, Cement Block, Safety Glasses, Face shield, Trusted Individual to Swing the Sledgehammer, For alternate version with bed of balloons:BalloonsWood BoardBalloon Cage, Balloons, Wood Board, Balloon Cage

title: Martian Hat
description: The martian hat is made of wire and two tennis balls.  It will balance on a person's head at the point in the middle but not if flipped upside down.  This can be done to discuss center of mass. Once the martian hat is balanced on an individual's head, the person can quickly rotate and the hat will remain stable while the person rotates beneath it. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the martian hat on the lab table. Place the martian hat on your head or a volunteer's head.  Have the person quickly spin. You may flip the hat over to discuss center of mass and why it will only balance in one position.
notes: This works best on someone with less hair or hair pulled smooth so that it does not bump the wire. This demonstration may require a little practice.
discussion_questions: What changes if you move slowly vs. move quickly? | How would this experiment change if you used heavier baseballs? What if we used lighter ping pong balls?
equipment: Martian Hat

title: Pull the Tablecloth
description: Using a quick pull, a tablecloth is pulled out from under dishes. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Cover the lab table with the tablecloth.  Place the dishes on top. Firmly grab the tablecloth and pull out and down to remove it from under the dishes.
notes: This demonstration requires some practice ahead of time. This demonstration has analternate version.Based on your proficiency, it may be easier to do this version or the other, or both. They demonstrate the same concept.
discussion_questions: Why must the table cloth be pulled quickly? | What if we replaced the nylon table cloth with a rough rug? What would change?Could we still make the demo work? How? | Could we still make the demo work? How? | Could we still make the demo work? How? | What if we used heavier objects on the table? What would change? | What if we used lighter objects? | What if we used lighter objects?
equipment: Tablecloth, Dishes and other tabletop items

title: Stacked Coke Bottles
description: Two Coke bottles are stacked with a dollar bill in between them and water in the top glass.  When the dollar is pulled out, the bottles remained stacked and the water drains into the bottom glass.  This can also be done with out the water.  Both demonstrate inertia just with a different mass on top. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Stack Coke bottles with dollar bill in between them.  Quickly pull the dollar out. This can be done with water in the top bottle as well.  The increase weight on top makes it a little easier and it looks cool!  Fill one bottle with water.  Place the dollar on top of this bottle followed by the other bottle.  Carefully turn over the system so that the filled bottle is on top.  Quickly pull out the dollar. The water will drain into the bottom bottle.
notes: It may be easier to strike the dollar downward with a pen to ensure a smooth pull. This demonstration requires some practice ahead of time. This demonstration has analternate version.Based on your proficiency, it may be easier to do this version or the other, or both. They demonstrate the same concept.
discussion_questions: Why can't we pull the dollar bill out slowly? | What if we replaced the dollar bill with a rubber sheet? What physical quantity would change? | How does the bottle being filled/not filled with water change the demo?
equipment: Two Glass Coke Bottles, One Dollar Bill, Water

title: Atwood's Machine
description: Two equal masses are connected with a string over a pulley.  If an additional small mass is added to one side, the system will accelerate in that direction.    This can also be setup with two pulleys.  Acceleration, Force, and Tension can be discussed when examining this system.
setup: Suspend the pulley above the lab table using the ring stand and clamps.  Tie a piece of string between the two mass hangers.  (Be sure it is an appropriate length so that one mass hanger can be on the table and the other still hangs below the pulley.) Place equal mass on the mass hangers.  The system will remain the same unless perturbed. Place an additional small mass on one side and that mass will accelerate downward. Include a spring scale for measuring force.
notes: None
equipment: Ring Stand with Clamp, Pulley, String, Spring Scale, Two Mass Hangers, Two Equal Masses (200 g), One Small Mass (20 g)

title: Cart Fan
description: When a fan on a cart is turned on, it puts a force on a mass of air. Obedient to Newton's Third law, the mass of air puts a force — directed in the opposite direction — onto the cart. The cart moves in the direction opposite to the direction of the force on the mass of air. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the cart fan on the track.Turn on the cart fan and watch it move across the track.
notes: None
discussion_questions: If all the propeller is doing is spinning, why does the cart move forward? | Is the air moving backward in response? | Is the air or the propeller experiencing a larger force? | What if we kept the cart in place? If the air is still getting pushed, is the cart still experiencing an equal and opposite force?What does that force do if the cart is not moving? | What does that force do if the cart is not moving? | What does that force do if the cart is not moving?
equipment: Cart Fan, Track, Sail

title: Flying Propeller
description: This demonstration shows rotational lift.  Pulling the string on this propeller causes it to rotate about a vertical axis. This forces the air downward and thus the propeller upward.  Bernoulli's Principle also applies in this situation as the air movement across the blades causes lower pressure above the blades and higher pressure below which generates lift.
setup: Place equipment on the lab table. Place the propeller on the launcher.  Quickly pull the string.  The propeller flies upward then floats to the ground.
notes: None
discussion_questions: If all the propeller is doing is spinning, why does it move upward? | Is the air moving downward in response? | Is the air or the propeller experiencing a larger force?
equipment: Propeller, Propeller Launcher (Pull String Device)

title: Atomic Model
description: By twisting and compressing the model, stress, strain, and shearing forces are easily visible.
setup: Place the model on the lab table. Twist, push, and manipulate the model to view the forces.
notes: None
equipment: Atomic Model

title: Happy and Sad Balls
description: This demonstration uses two balls that look very similar but have different elasticity.  When the balls are dropped, one experiences an elastic collision and the other an inelastic collision.  In the inelastic collision, the kinetic energy is converted to heat and the ball doesn't bounce much.  In the elastic collision, little heat is produced so the ball bounces close to its' original height. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the balls on the lab table.  Make sure they can't roll off. Drop the balls at the same time and observe as one bounces and one settles and does not bounce.
notes: None
discussion_questions: (Before demos) Which ball will bounce higher? | What causes one ball to bounce higher than the other? | Is momentum conserved in both situations? Is energy? If not, where does the energy go?
equipment: Arbor Scientific Happy and Sad Balls

title: Spring Constant
description: This demonstration shows how the mass hung from a spring affects the length of the spring. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Hang the spring from the ring stand.  A mass hanger should be hung from the spring. Setup a meter stick so that it is lined up with the bottom of the mass hanger.  Setup the webcam so that it views the meter stick and is connected to the projector. Add mass to the mass hanger to see the length of the spring change.  The displacement can be measured on the meter stick.
notes: None
discussion_questions: Will changing the mass affect the spring constant? | How do we define x in F=-kx? Why is there a negative sign?
equipment: Ring Stand and Clamps, Spring, Mass Hanger, Masses, Meter Stick, Webcam, Demo Computer or Laptop

title: Flame Tornado
description: This demonstration show conservation of angular momentum as flames from a bowl of burning alcohol spiral upward.  As the hot air rises, the flames move upward and spin about the bowl of alcohol. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the turntable on the lab bench.  Place the aluminum cover on the turntable and the stainless steel dish in the center of the cover.  Place the cage on the turntable and secure it with the band clamp. Pour a small amount of denatured alcohol in the dish.  (Hint: a little bit goes a long way!) Carefully light the alcohol, close and lock the cage door. Spin the turntable to watch the flames spiral upward. Once complete, let the alcohol burn off before disassembly.
notes: Be sure to have a fire extinguisher. Make sure everything is secure before spinning. It is important to get the bowl centered on the turntable for the best effect.
discussion_questions: Will this experiment work if the flame is not centered? | Will this experiment work without the mesh? | Is the angular momentum of the air in the tornado increasing or decreasing?
equipment: Large Turntable, Aluminum Turntable Cover, Metal Cage, Special Band Clamp, Stainless Steel Bowl, Denatured Alcohol, Lighter or Matches, Fire Extinguisher

title: Moment of Inertia Race
description: This demonstration allows for comparison of objects with different mass distributions.  The angular accelerations are compared for objects with a different moment of inertia.  As two objects race down the ramp, the one with the most mass concentrated at the center will win. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Set up a ramp on the lab table.  Set the cylindrical objects next to it. Select two objects.  Place them at the top of the ramp and release.  Stop the objects at the bottom of the ramp. Repeat this process to compare objects of the same mass or shape but different mass distribution.
notes: None
discussion_questions: Does total mass affect rolling speed? | Which one will reach the end first? Which one will reach the end last?
equipment: Ramp, Various Cylindrical Objects (Stored Together)

title: Moment of Inertia Rods
description: In this demonstration, students try to rotate two rods of the same mass.  One is much easier to rotate than the other as their masses are concentrated differently.  This gives the rods different moments of inertia.
setup: Place the moment of inertia rods on the lab table. The instructor will need one or two student volunteers.  The student should grip the rod at its center and try to rotate it as quickly as possible. The red rod is much easier to rotate as the mass is concentrated at its center.  The yellow rod has mass concentrated at its ends, therefore it has a greater moment of inertia and is harder to rotate.
notes: None
discussion_questions: If the mass of the two rods is the same, does mass alone affect how easy a rod is to spin? | Which rod is harder to spin? | What is different about the two rods? | Where is the mass concentrated in rod 1? | Where is the mass concentrated in rod 2?
equipment: Red Moment of Inertia Rod, Yellow Moment of Inertia Rod

title: Precession of Spinning Gyroscope
description: A bicycle wheel is suspended from the ceiling.  After spinning it very quickly and held horizontal, the wheel will process around the center string despite gravity pulling it down.  This is due to the angular momentum and torque on the wheel. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Hang the bicycle wheel from the hooks in the ceiling. Hold the axle and use the dremel to spin the wheel.  After a few seconds, hold the wheel horizontal and release it. The wheel precesses as it spins.
notes: Be sure to clear the area around the hanging wheel so that it has room to move.
discussion_questions: Why does the wheel take so long to move downward? | Will the precession go in the same or opposite direction of the spin of the wheel? (This can be asked after the inital demo since they probably weren't paying too much attention to the directions of spin) | Will this work if both sides of the wheel are held up by a string?
equipment: Bicycle Wheel with White Wooden Stand, Rope, Dremel

title: Rotating Stool with Hand Weights
description: This demonstration shows Conservation of Angular Momentum.  An individual sits in the chair holding the hand weights with arms extended.  This person is slowly rotated.  If they pull their arms into their chest, the rotation speeds up.  If the arms are extended again, the rotation slows back to the original speed. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the rotating stool platform and hand weights at the front of the room.  Do not leave it on the cart! A person should sit on the stool holding the hand weights with their arms extended.  Start the stool slowly spinning.  The person should bring their arms into their chest.  They will spin faster.  If they extend their arms again, they will slow down.
notes: Remove the stool from the cart before using. Be careful not to fall off the stool. The person will usually feel a Coriolis Force.
discussion_questions: As the masses move inward, does the angular momentum increase or decrease?What about the moment of inertia?What about the angular velocity? | What about the moment of inertia?What about the angular velocity? | What about the moment of inertia? | What about the angular velocity?
equipment: Rotating Stool Platform, Hand weights

title: Rotating Stool with Spinning Wheel
description: This demonstration shows Conservation of Angular Momentum.  A person sits on the stool platform and holds a spinning wheel.  If they change the orientation of the wheel, the person will rotate so that the total angular momentum of the system remains the same. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the rotating stool platform and bicycle wheel at the front of the room. Do not leave it on the cart! A person should sit on the stool holding the bicycle wheel upright.  Start the bicycle wheel spinning in the vertical plane..  The person should rotate the wheel in to the horizontal plane in one direction.  The stool and person will rotate.  If they return the bicycle wheel to its' original orientation they will stop.  The wheel can be turned horizontally in the other way to see the system spin in the opposite direction. This can also be started horizontal plane and turned all the way over.
notes: Be sure that the person with the bicycle wheel does not have any loose clothing that could get caught in the wheel. Be careful not to fall off the stool.
discussion_questions: Which way will the person spin compared to the spinning of the wheel? | If the person puts the wheel back upright, why do they stop? | Which physical quantity is being conserved? | What are some real-world applications of this phenomenon?
equipment: Rotating Stool Platform, Bicycle Wheel, Dremel (optional)

description: More Information Coming Soon. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Coming Soon

title: Spinning Hoberman Sphere
description: A Hoberman Sphere is a collapsible sphere toy.  It is hung from a stand and slowly rotated.  When a string is pulled to collapse the sphere, it will rotate much faster due to Conservation of Angular Momentum. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Hang the Hoberman sphere from a tall ring stand setup so that it can spin freely and the string hanging out of the bottom is easily accessible. Give the sphere a push to start it slowly spinning.  Pull the string to collapse the sphere and see it spin faster.  Release the string and the sphere will return to its' original size and speed of rotation.
notes: Be careful not to pinch anything in the collapsing sphere.
discussion_questions: What real life example does this remind you of? (answers can include ballet, playground equipment, etc.) | Can this explain why our solar system or planets spin? | Is this an example of conservation of angular momentum or energy?
equipment: Hoberman Sphere with String Attached, Tall Ring Stand, Swivel Coupling

title: Double Cone Runs Up a Track
description: When the double cone is placed at the narrow end of the track, it appears to roll uphill.  In reality, the center of mass is actually going downhill. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the track, cone, and rod on the lab table. When the rod is placed on the track it rolls down the track.  When the double cone is placed on the track, it appears to roll up the track.
notes: None
discussion_questions: Where is the center of mass of this system? How does it move? | Is the cone actually moving upwards?
equipment: Wood Triangular Track, Wood Double Cone, Piece of Pipe or Rod

title: Grip Bar
description: This demonstration conveys static torque.  As mass is added far from the handle, torque will cause the object to rotate.
setup: Place the equipment on the lab table. A student holds the grip bar by its handle.  The instructor hangs the weight close to the handle.  Nothing happens. The instructor hangs the weight farther from the handle.  Their grip slips and the bar rotates.
notes: What is the torque on the bar from the weight in each situation? What is the net torque on the system in each situation? What causes the bar to stay in place for the first few positions? What changes when it moves? What has been overcome?
equipment: Grip Bar Apparatus, 0.5 kg Mass

title: Hanging Block
description: This demonstration again shows the resolution of forces on an object.  Though it appears the block is sitting on the ramp, it is actually being supported by the two strings.  Calculations can be done to determine the forces involved.
setup: Setup the equipment as shown in the first photo above.  It should appear that the block rests on the ramp. Remove the ramp to show that the block is hanging (as shown in the second photo).
notes: Ensure that the strings attached to the block are perpendicular to each other. If the strings will slide along the hooks so that the angle between them is no longer ninety degrees, the angle of the stand is no longer equal to any angle when decomposing the tensions into horizontal and vertical components.
discussion_questions: What is the net force on the system? | What are the individual forces acting on the system? | What is the tension in string 1 if you calculate it from a free-body diagram? Does it match the weight of its hanging block? | What is the tension in string 2 if you calculate it from a free-body diagram? Does it match the weight of its hanging block?
equipment: Ring Stands, 1 kg Block, String, Two Pulleys, Ramp, Protractor, Masses and Mass Hangers

title: Irregular Object
description: This demonstration shows how to find the center of mass for an irregularly shaped object.
setup: Hang Irregular Objects on Ring Stands through one of their holes.  Hang a plum bob from the same hole. Use chalk to trace the plum bob line through the object.  Hang the object from a different hole and repeat this process until you have used all the holes.  The center of mass is the intersection of all these lines.
notes: None
discussion_questions: Where does gravity act on a rigid object? | Why is the center of mass along the line of the hanging string? | What would happen to the object if the center of mass was off to the side? What would the free-body diagram look like in this instance?
equipment: Ring Stand, Irregular Shaped Objects Pieces, Plum Bob, Chalk

title: Loaded Beam
description: This demonstration is used to calculate the forces holding up a beam.  As masses are rearranged, students calculate the tension in the strings to keep the beam from falling or rotating.
setup: Set up the equipment from the Klinger Magnetic Mechanics Kit as shown in the image above. The instructor can change the location of the masses and have students calculate the tension in the strings.
notes: None
discussion_questions: What is the net force in each situation? What is the net torque? | What are the tensions in the strings in each situation? If we added a spring scale, is that what we would measure? (can actually do this!)
equipment: Klinger Magnetic Mechanics Kit, String

title: Meter Stick Balance
description: This demonstration shows torque and equilibrium.  A meter stick is balanced on a stand.  Mass can be hung at different distances and on both sides of the pivot point.  Depending on the sum of the torques the meter stick can be balanced. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place meter stick balance stand on a lab jack or stand if necessary and on a lab table. Put meter stick clamp without hanger on the meter stick along with clamps with hangers.  Suspend the meter stick on the stand. Hang mass hangers and masses until the system balances.
notes: None
discussion_questions: Can we have more mass on one end of the meter stick and have it remain balanced? | Can we have the pivot at a location other than the center and have it remain balanced? | When do we need to account for the weight of the meter stick? | What is the net force on the system? The net torque? | Why would the net force not help us solve most problems? | Can ask: where a mass needs to be positioned to balance, where the pivot needs to be positioned. | How does this relate to center of mass?
equipment: Meter Stick, Meter Stick Balance Stand, At least 2 Meter Stick Clamps with Hangers, 1 Meter Stick Clamp without a Hanger, Mass Hangers, Assorted Masses, Lab Jack or Stand

title: Model Arm
description: In this model of the human bicep-arm system, a rod pivots about one of its ends as shown in the photo. Approximately 10 cm from that end, tension in a chain exerts a measurable force on the rod. Also, masses on a mass hanger loads down the rod's farther end. Students determine the value of tension read on the spring scale.
setup: Set up the equipment as shown in the image above. Add masses and take measurements.  Have students calculate the tension in the spring.
notes: None
discussion_questions: What is the net force in each situation? The net torque? | Why can't we use the net force to calculate the tension in the string? | Do we need to know the mass of the rod?
equipment: Ring Stand, Bar for Model Arm, Spring Scale with Chain, Masses and Mass Hangers, Meter Stick, Protractor

title: Resolution of Forces
description: This demonstration gives a visualization and verification of how to resolve forces into components.  Students can calculate and see the readings on the scales.
setup: Using the Klinger Magnetic Mechanics Kit, arrange the equipment as shown in the photo above. Calculations may be done to verify the scale readings.
notes: May take a few minutes to setup.
discussion_questions: What magnitude of force makes up the horizontal component of the cord's tension? | What magnitude of force makes up the vertical component of the cord's tension?
equipment: Klinger Magnetic Mechanics Kit, String, Protractor

title: Roberval Balance
description: This demonstration shows static torque for a more complicated system.  Students can calculate the torque at different positions on the balance to see why it levels out in certain cases.
setup: Place the balance and masses on the lab table. If equal masses are placed on the yellow platforms, the system looks unbalanced. The instructor places a set of masses on one side's outer platform, and an equal set on the other side's inner platform, as shown in the photo. The balance levels out.
notes: The calculations involved with this demonstration can take considerable time.  Therefore, it might best be done as a homework problem.
discussion_questions: What is the net force in the system in each case? The net torque? | Does the net force in the x-direction help you solve this problem? | Can you solve the system using one rod?
equipment: Roberval Balance Apparatus, Masses (Two Equal Sets)

title: The Leaning Tower
description: This leaning tower stands upright initially.  When the hat is placed on top it falls over because the center of gravity is located outside of the tower.
setup: Place the equipment on the lab table. The tower stays upright despite the fact that it is slanted to one side.  Place the hat on top of it and it falls over.
notes: None.
discussion_questions: What causes something to tip over or remain upright? | How would we prevent the tower from tipping?What have we changed by doing so? How does this relate to question 1? | What have we changed by doing so? How does this relate to question 1? | What have we changed by doing so? How does this relate to question 1?
equipment: Leaning Tower Base, Leaning Tower Hat

title: Ball on a Looped Track
description: This demonstration conveys conservation of energy.  If the ball is not started with enough potential energy (high enough along the track), it will not complete the loop.  Kinetic and potential energy can be discussed as well as friction while analyzing how the type of energy changes while the total energy remains the same. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the track on the lab table.  Place the ball at the bottom of the track so it does not roll away. Hold the ball along the long end of the track and release to see if it completes the loop.  Repeat as necessary.  Please try to catch the balls as quickly as possible throughout this demo.
notes: The track should be marked at 2R, 2.5R, and 2.7R.
discussion_questions: What height will cause the ball to complete the loop and reach the end? | What speed does the ball need to maintain circular motion? | What are the potential and kinetic energies throughout the motion?
equipment: Loop the Loop Track, Smooth Ball (Billiard, metal, bouncy etc.)

title: Bowling Ball on a String
description: A bowling ball on a cable is hung from the ceiling.  When the ball is pulled back and released it will move like a giant pendulum returning almost to its starting position.  This demonstrates Conservation of Energy.  There is a small loss due to friction and air resistance so the bowling ball will not make it all the way back to it's starting position. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Hang the bowling ball on the cable from the track in the ceiling of the room. Pull the ball back to some fixed position.  Release the ball and watch it travel away and back almost to its' starting position.
notes: Do not push the ball or it will hit you!  Just release the ball! Make sure the cable is securely fastened to the ball and to the track at the ceiling of the room.
discussion_questions: Why can the ball never get higher than its starting position? | What would cause it to go higher?
equipment: Bowling Ball on a Cable

title: Chaotic (Double) Pendulum
description: This demonstration shows a double pendulum. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: If Chaotic Apparatus is not available: Use the string and balls to create pendulums. Hang the pendulum from the ring stand using the burette clamp. Hang a second pendulum from the first pendulum.
notes: Coming Soon
equipment: Chaotic Pendulum apparatus, Ring Stand, String, Two balls

title: Energy Change
description: This demonstration is used to discuss Conservation of Energy and how energy changes forms during motion.  A flexible curve is used to create a u-shaped channel were a ball rolls.  The curve is placed on an incline so that as the ball rolls, the potential energy changes to kinetic and back to potential.  The curve can be molded into different shapes as well.
setup: Place the clear plastic board under the document camera at an incline using a block. Bend the curve into the desired shape. Place the ball at the top of the curve and release it.
notes: None
discussion_questions: What are the components of energy in this system? | What does each component look like over time? | What does the total energy look like over time? | Depending on the shape, do we predict we reach the same height, or a different one? What if the shape isn't symmetric? What if we used a different mass?
equipment: Plastic Board, Wood Block or Lab Jack, Flexible Curve, Small Ball

title: PE to KE
description: This demonstration uses a glider on an air track to study conservation of energy.  As the glider accelerates down the air track due to gravity, Potential Energy is Converted to Kinetic Energy.  By tracking the glider's motion, calculations of the kinetic and potential energy can be done to show conservation of energy.
setup: Place the air track on a lab jack to create an incline. Connect the motion sensor to the Pasco interface. Connect the interface to the computer. Connect the demo computer to the projector system. Mount the motion sensor above the air track aligned with the sail on the glider using the ring stand. Open the Pasco data collection software and create graphs of position vs. time, and velocity vs. time. Turn on the air track.  Place the glider on the air track at a noted position.  Start the data collection.  Release the glider and let it move one meter down the track.  Stop the data collection.  Use the graphs to analyze and calculate the PE and KE to see if energy is conserved.
notes: None
discussion_questions: What is the KE at the beginning of the motion? What is the PE?What about at the end of the motion? | What about at the end of the motion? | What about at the end of the motion? | Is the total energy throughout the motion conserved?Where would it go if it wasn't? | Where would it go if it wasn't? | Where would it go if it wasn't?
equipment: Demo Computer or Laptop, Air Track, Pasco Interface, Motion Sensor, Glider with Sail, Ring Stand, Lab Jack or Block

title: Interrupted Pendulum
description: This demonstration shows conservation of energy for a pendulum.  When the pendulum is released, even though its path is interrupted, the pendulum still returns to its original height.
setup: Setup the system as shown in the image above. Pull the pendulum back to a height corresponding to the 20 cm mark on the scale.  Release the pendulum.  It will swing and hit the bar, but the mass will continue to travel up to a height corresponding to the 20 cm mark.
notes: It is best to use these values as different heights and setups could lead to slack in the string.
discussion_questions: (before demo) Will a regular pendulum reach the same height as the start, a lower, or a higher height? | (before demo) Will the interrupted pendulum reach the same height as the start, a lower, or a higher height? | What does the energy look like throughout this motion?
equipment: Klinger Mangetic Mechanics Kit, String, Large Nut, Webcam (optional)

title: Wilberforce Pendulum
description: The Wilberforce pendulum is a bob with masses on the side to give it a large moment of inertia. The pendulum demonstrates conservation of energy as it oscillates between two modes: one is the up-and-down motion of a mass on a spring, while the other is the spinning motion of a torsional pendulum. If the bob is pulled down and released it will begin to oscillate up and down. Shortly after, it will begin to rotate. Because the total energy of the system is constant, as the rotation speeds up the up and down oscillation loses amplitude.  Eventually, the bob seems to only spin.  It then begins oscillating up and down as the rotation slows until it is no longer spinning and has a large vertical amplitude.  This alternation continues. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Hang the pendulum from the ring stand using the burette clamp. Pull down on the bob and release to see the oscillations.
notes: Too large of an initial amplitude will not produce good results but too small of an amplitude will damp out very quickly.  May require a little practice.
discussion_questions: What are the components of the total energy of this system? | What does each component look like over time? | What does the total energy look like over time?
equipment: Ring Stand, Burette Clamp, Wilberforce Pendulum

title: Absorption Spectra
description: This demonstration shows the absorption of colors of the spectrum.  A beam of white light is passed through a diffraction grating to produce the continuous spectrum.  When a pair of glass blowing safety glasses is placed in front of the light, specific colors are absorbed (the yellow section).
setup: Place the light source on the demo table with the optics stand in front of it. Mount the diffraction film on the frame and place it in the holder. Turn on the light source and shine it through the diffraction grating to produce the continuous spectrum. Hold the glasses in front of the light source to see the absorption.
notes: None
equipment: Large Silver Light Source, Diffraction Film, Optics Frame and Stand, Special Safety Glasses

title: Phosphorescence
description: This demonstration is used to show how phosphorescent coatings work.  UV light is shown on phosphorescent paper.  The paper glows and continues to glow after the light is turned off.  Objects can be placed on the paper to reveal shadows.
setup: Place the phosphorescent paper and UV lamp on the demo table. Shine the light on the paper for a few seconds.  DO NOT SHINE THE LIGHT AT ANYONE!  UV LIGHT IS DAMAGING TO THE EYES! Turn off the lights to see the paper glow. Place an object on top of the paper.  Shine the light on the paper for a seconds.  remove the object to reveal the shadow on the paper.
notes: None
equipment: Phosphorescent Paper, UV Lamp, Various Objects (Optional)

title: Spectrum Chart
description: The poster is used as a visual aid to assist in the explanation of the different types of spectra that exist and to give concrete examples of what different types of spectra look like.​
setup: Hang the chart for easy viewing.
notes: None
equipment: Spectrum Chart, Hooks or stand to hang chart

title: Spectrum Tubes
description: This demonstration show the atomic spectrum of various elements.  There are several gas discharge tubes available that when excited by the power supply, give off atomic spectra. The spectra can be viewed with diffraction gratings. ​A chart of spectra for some elements is also available.
setup: Place the requested spectrum tubes in power supplies on the table. Place the diffraction gratings on the table. Look at the illuminated tube through the diffraction grating to view the spectrum.  It may appear off to the side. The gases available are Hydrogen, Helium, Neon, Nitrogen, and Mercury.
notes: None
equipment: Spectrum Tubes mounted in Power Supplies, Diffraction Gratings, Spectra Chart

title: Cloud Chamber
description: This demonstration is used to show the detection of subatomic and high energy particles. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Get dry ice. Set cloud chamber apparatus on the demo table and level it. Place the dry ice slab under the clear box.  Again, make sure the box is level.  Consider wrapping the dry ice area with bubble wrap and securing with rubber bands and clips. Soak the felt of the inside of the box with ethanol.  Pour a small amount of ethanol in the bottom of the chamber. Align a light to shine on the ethanol in the bottom of the chamber. After cooling, small tracks will be visible. A webcam may be setup to project a view of the chamber.
notes: Be careful when handling dry ice.  Be sure to use gloves.
equipment: Cloud Chamber Apparatus, Dry Ice, Dry Ice Gloves, Ethanol, Bubble Wrap, Rubber Bands and Paper Clips, Lamp with Stand, Web Cam (Optional)

title: Radiation Detection and Sources
description: This demonstration shows a radioactive source and its detection.  The plate is coated in Uranium Oxide which gives it the orange color.  Using a Geiger Counter you can hear the detection of radioactive particles (alpha in this case).  The Altimeter was manufactured for use during World War II.  The paint contains radium which emits alpha, beta, and gamma radiation. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the sources and the Geiger Counter on the demo table. Turn the dial on the Geiger Counter to the x10 setting and turn the Audio on. Bring the detector near the sources to hear the counts of radioactive particles.
notes: None
equipment: Geiger Counter, Fiesta Ware Lid, World War II Altimeter

title: Microwave Tunneling
description: This demonstration illustrates the principle of quantum tunneling using microwaves and wax prisms.  First, microwaves are sent across a space to a detector.  The detector registers a reading. Then, a wax prism is inserted between the generator and detector.  The detector now reads zero.  If the detector is moved to the other side of the prism is will show a reading again.  This shows total internal reflection.  If the detector is returned to its original position and a second prism is placed on the other side of the first, the detector will show a reading if the gap between the prisms is small enough.  At this point, the photons are able to tunnel under the gap into the second prism and continue on to the detector. This phenomenon of photons traveling through the gap is known as quantum tunneling. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information below and images above for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the microwave transmitter on a flat surface. Place a microwave receiver directly across from the microwave transmitter. If the height of the receiver is not aligned with the height of the transmitter, then place some object beneath the receiver until is is perfectly level. Turn on the receiver. Turn on the transmitter by plugging it in and rotating the dial. Adjust the power dials as needed until the desired signal strength is reached. Thereceiverwill register a reading.Depending on the strength of the signal, turn the receiver to the appropriate multiplier (where the signal reads between the maximum and minimum). Place a wax prism between the transmitter and receiver.  The receiver should read zero.  Rotate the receiver around the prism.  You should get a reading at the point of total internal reflection. Return the detector to its original position.  Turn on and place the other receiver at the point of total internal reflection that was previously observed. Make the second receiver level with the transmitter's signal. The detector will register a reading if the gap is small enough.  As the gap narrows, the detector reading should increase.
notes: While the receivers can be used in a more qualitative, observational manner, precise quantitative data can be collected. Simply use banana plugs to attach the transmitters to the current sensors and connect the current sensor to a device equipped with PASCO Capstone software. If using this method of observation, the multipliers on the receivers become even more important. ND Demos primarily used a multiplier of 10. The volume dial has no effect on the microwave emissions. Itis onlyon the transmitterto serve as an auditory signal that the transmitter is operating correctly. If unsure of the strength of the microwave emissions, use the volume as a tool. The volume can get very loud quite quickly, so be sensitive with any volume adjustments. The microwave transmitter has many dials and attachments that impact the emitted signal. To make the signal at its strongest, rotate the attenuator so that it hits the leftmost boundary (as seen in the above image).
equipment: Microwave transmitter, Microwave receivers (x2), Receiver stands (x2), Plug-in transformer, Belz microwave emitter attachment, Budd-Stanley curved waveguide, Circular waveguide, Dielectric waveguide, Wax prisms (x2) (may not be kept with kit), Grid, Small plastic screws (x7), Reflective metal plate, Banana plugs (x4) (optional), PASCO current sensor (x2) (optional)

title: Photoelectric Effect
description: This demonstration shows the photoelectric effect through the production of photoelectrons in zinc.  When ultraviolet light is shown on a negatively charged zinc plate attached to an electroscope, the scope discharges. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the electroscope, UV lamp, and rod with rubber on the demo table. Shortly before the demo is done, clean the zinc plate with steel wool or sandpaper to remove the zinc oxide. Attach the zinc plate to the electroscope. Charge the electroscope using the rod and rubber. Shine the ultraviolet light on the zinc plate.  BE SURE NOT TO SHINE THE LIGHT AT ANYONE AS UV LIGHT IS DAMAGING TO HUMAN EYES!
notes: There is a slight delay with the lamp turning on. A Plexiglas plate can be placed between the lamp and plate to show that it is the light causing the discharge. A webcam may be setup to view the electroscope.
equipment: Electroscope, Zinc Plate, Ebonite Rod, Rubber, UVC Lamp, Webcam (optional)

If two perpendicular polarizers are placed behind the wire, the interference pattern disappears as the photons are labeled.  If a third polarizer is placed in the path of the beam and rotated, the pattern interference pattern will reappear at certain angles as the labels are erased. * Equipment seen in the video may vary from equipment used in ND Demonstrations.  See information and images below for ND equipment and setup.
setup: Place the optical rail on the demo table. Mount the two optics post holders on the rail close to one end. Mount the laser in it's holder and in the burette clamp.  Place this in the first post holder. Attach the polarizers and wire to the screen.  Place the screen in the second post holder. Align the laser so it strikes the center of the wire.  This should create a fuzzy pattern. Hold a polarizer in between the screen and the wall and rotate it to see the different patterns.
notes: Do not shine the laser at anyone!
equipment: Red/Green Laser, Optics Rail, Two Optics Post Holders, Burette Clamp, Optics Screen with Hole, Two Polarizers and Wire Attachment, Laser Holder, Additional Poarizers

title: Interferometry
description: This demonstration shows the Michelson interferometer which produces interference fringes by splitting a beam of monochromatic light so that one beam strikes a fixed mirror and the other a movable mirror. When the reflected beams are brought back together, an interference pattern results from the differences in path lengths traveled. A Michelson interferometer with a green laser but without a viewing screen. The JDSU laser unit is simply used to block the green laser from traveling farther into the room. A Michelson interferometer with a red laser. Instead of a viewing screen attached to the interferometer base, this setup uses a clipboard at a greater distance to see a larger image of the interference patterns. The interference patters of a red laser with a Michelson interferometer.
setup: This demo may take some time to set-up. While there aren't many steps to get the interferometer running, they can take many tries to get right. Carefully watch the above video and try to follow along with the kit. If there are any difficulties, see thePrecision Interferometer Manualfor troubleshooting advice.
notes: The PASCO precision interferometer can be used with a variety of interferometer types. The Michelson method is discussed in the video above, while the Fabry-Perot is briefly mentioned. The kit is compatible with Michelson, Fabry-Perot, and Twyman–Green setups. Multiple experiments can be performed with this interferometer. Some examples are measuring the wavelength of the light source, the index of refraction of air, and the index of refraction of glass. For more information on how to assemble the various interferometer setups and conduct the recommended experiments, please see thePrecision Interferometer Manual.
